name: Learn: CNI & Cluster Networking
objective: CKA › Services & Networking (20%) + Troubleshooting (30%). Goal: understand the CNI that gives pods IPs, recover a node whose CNI config is missing, and verify the DNS + Service datapath (CoreDNS, kube-proxy, pod-to-pod).
description: How pods actually get networking on a real cluster — the CNI, and how to diagnose and fix it, plus the CoreDNS + Service datapath.

questions.title: The CNI gives pods their IPs
questions.teach:
Kubernetes doesn't do pod networking itself — a **CNI plugin** does. The kubelet calls the plugin (via config in `/etc/cni/net.d/` + binaries in `/opt/cni/bin/`) to attach each pod to the network and hand it an IP from the **pod CIDR**. On kind that plugin is **kindnet**, running as a DaemonSet; common alternatives are **Calico**, **Cilium**, **Flannel**, and **Weave**, each typically shipped as its own DaemonSet in `kube-system`.

**The Kubernetes network model (what any CNI must satisfy):**
- Every pod gets its own IP.
- Pods on any node can reach pods on any other node **without NAT**.
- A pod sees its own IP the same way others see it.

**Where to look when networking is involved:**
- `kubectl get pod -o wide` — shows the pod IP and the node it landed on.
- The pod CIDR vs the **Service CIDR** are different ranges (e.g. `10.244.0.0/16` for pods vs `10.96.0.0/12` for Services) — don't confuse a pod IP with a Service clusterIP.
- CNI DaemonSet pods live in `kube-system`; `kubectl -n kube-system get ds` lists them.

**Exam gotchas:**
- No CNI (or a broken CNI config) → no pod IP → pods stay `ContainerCreating` / `Pending`, and `kubectl describe pod` shows a `NetworkPlugin`/`cni` error event.
- A freshly `kubeadm init`'d control-plane node stays `NotReady` until a CNI is installed — that's expected, not a bug.
- Pod IPs are ephemeral: they change on restart/reschedule, which is exactly why Services (stable virtual IPs) exist.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `cni-learn`, run a pod named `netcheck` (image `busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`). Confirm the CNI gave it an IP.

Target: `netcheck` is `Running` with a `.status.podIP`.
questions.hint: `kubectl run netcheck -n cni-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --command -- sleep 3600`, then `kubectl get pod netcheck -n cni-learn -o wide`.
questions.solution:
kubectl run netcheck -n cni-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --command -- sleep 3600
kubectl get pod netcheck -n cni-learn -o wide   # has an IP, Running

verification.description: netcheck is Running with a CNI-assigned IP

questions.title: Recover a node with a missing CNI config
questions.teach:
A classic break: a node's CNI config is gone (`/etc/cni/net.d/10-kindnet.conflist` deleted), so new pods there can't get networking and sit `Pending`/`ContainerCreating`. The kindnet DaemonSet **reinstalls that config when its pod starts** — so restarting the kindnet pod on the affected node restores networking. (Same idea for Calico/Cilium/Flannel: their node agent writes the CNI conf on startup.) **How to diagnose a networking break:** - `kubectl describe pod

` — look for events like `failed to find plugin`, `cni config uninitialized`, or `NetworkPlugin cni failed`. - `kubectl get nodes` — a node with a dead CNI often shows `NotReady` with a `KubeletNotReady` / `cni plugin not initialized` condition. - `kubectl -n kube-system get pods -o wide` — confirm the CNI DaemonSet pod on that node is actually `Running`. - Two layers to check: the **config** (`/etc/cni/net.d/`) and the **binaries** (`/opt/cni/bin/`). **Ways to restart / reconcile the CNI pod on one node:** - `kubectl -n kube-system delete pod -l --field-selector spec.nodeName=` — the DaemonSet recreates it immediately, rewriting the conf. - `kubectl -n kube-system rollout restart ds/` — restarts it on **every** node (heavier, but fine if you don't need to target one). **Exam gotchas:** - `--field-selector spec.nodeName=` targets the single broken node — don't nuke the whole DaemonSet when only one node is affected. - It takes a few seconds (~15s) for the new pod to start and rewrite the config; re-check with `-o wide` rather than assuming it failed. - A DaemonSet pod can't be `scale`d (there's no replica count) — you restart it by deleting the pod or rolling the DaemonSet. - If the **binaries** under `/opt/cni/bin/` are missing (not just the conf), restarting the agent may not help — the CNI image has to repopulate them, or they must be restored on the host.
questions.prompt:
The CNI config was removed on node `$W2`, and pod `netbroken` (pinned to `$W2`) is stuck with no IP. Restore networking so `netbroken` gets an IP.

Target: `netbroken` has a `.status.podIP`.
questions.hint: Reinstall the config by restarting kindnet on that node: `kubectl -n kube-system delete pod -l app=kindnet --field-selector spec.nodeName=$W2` (the new kindnet pod rewrites /etc/cni/net.d). Give it ~15s.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n kube-system delete pod -l app=kindnet --field-selector spec.nodeName=kindlab-worker2
# kindnet restarts and reinstalls /etc/cni/net.d/10-kindnet.conflist; netbroken then gets an IP
kubectl get pod netbroken -n cni-learn -o wide

verification.description: CNI restored on $W2 — netbroken now has an IP

questions.title: CoreDNS resolves Service names
questions.teach:
**CoreDNS** (a Deployment in `kube-system`, fronted by the `kube-dns` Service at the cluster DNS IP, usually `10.96.0.10`) answers in-cluster DNS. The kubelet injects that DNS IP and a `search` list into every pod's `/etc/resolv.conf`.

**DNS names you should know:**
- Services: `<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local` → the Service's clusterIP.
- **Headless** Services (`clusterIP: None`): the name returns the backing pod IPs (A records), one per endpoint.
- Pods (rarely needed): `<pod-ipv4-dashed>.<ns>.pod.cluster.local` (e.g. `10-244-1-5.cni-learn.pod.cluster.local`).
- **SRV** records exist for named ports: `_<port>._<proto>.<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local`.

**How short names resolve:** the `search` domains (`<ns>.svc.cluster.local`, `svc.cluster.local`, `cluster.local`) let a pod use `web` or `web.cni-learn` from within its own namespace. `ndots:5` in resolv.conf means names with fewer than 5 dots try the search list first.

**Ways to test DNS:**
- `nslookup <name>` or `kubectl exec <pod> -- nslookup <name>`.
- `kubectl run tmp --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- nslookup <name>` then read its logs.
- `dig`/`host` if the image has them.

**Exam gotchas:**
- busybox `nslookup` is unreliable with the search list — use the **FQDN** `<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local` to test deterministically.
- `NXDOMAIN` for a Service name usually means the Service doesn't exist / wrong namespace; for a short name it often means you relied on the search list. A timeout (not NXDOMAIN) points at CoreDNS being down or a NetworkPolicy blocking egress to `kube-system:53` (udp **and** tcp).
- Check CoreDNS health with `kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=kube-dns` and `kubectl -n kube-system logs deploy/coredns`.
- A pod's `dnsPolicy` matters: `ClusterFirst` (default) uses CoreDNS; `Default` uses the node's resolver; `None` + `dnsConfig` lets you set it manually.
questions.prompt:
Run a pod named `dnscheck` (image `busybox:1.36`) that resolves the kubernetes API Service by its FQDN `kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local`.

Target: `dnscheck`'s logs show a resolved `Address` for that name (no NXDOMAIN).
questions.hint: `kubectl run dnscheck -n cni-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never --command -- nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local`, then `kubectl logs dnscheck -n cni-learn`.
questions.solution:
kubectl run dnscheck -n cni-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never --command -- nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local
kubectl logs dnscheck -n cni-learn   # Address: 10.96.0.1

questions.title: Expose a Deployment (kube-proxy wires it up)
questions.teach:
A **Service** gets a stable virtual IP (clusterIP); **kube-proxy** programs each node (iptables or IPVS rules) so traffic to that IP load-balances to the backing pods. The Service's **Endpoints** / **EndpointSlices** list is the proof its `selector` matched `Ready` pods.

**Service types:**
- **ClusterIP** (default) — reachable only inside the cluster.
- **NodePort** — also opens a port on every node (range **30000–32767**); still has a clusterIP.
- **LoadBalancer** — provisions an external LB; also has a NodePort and a clusterIP underneath.
- **ExternalName** — a CNAME to an external DNS name; no proxying, no selector.
- **Headless** (`clusterIP: None`) — no virtual IP; DNS returns the pod IPs directly.

**Ports — three distinct things:**
- `port` — the port the Service listens on.
- `targetPort` — the port on the pod it forwards to (defaults to `port`; can be a named port).
- `nodePort` — the node-level port (NodePort/LoadBalancer only).

**Ways to create a Service:**
- `kubectl expose deployment/<d> --port=80 [--target-port=8080] [--type=NodePort]`.
- `kubectl create service clusterip <name> --tcp=80:8080`.
- A YAML manifest with `spec.selector` + `spec.ports`.
- **Selector-less** Service + a hand-authored EndpointSlice to point at arbitrary IPs (e.g. an external DB).

**Exam gotchas:**
- **No endpoints** almost always = the Service `selector` doesn't match the pod labels, or the pods aren't `Ready` (readiness probe failing). Verify with `kubectl get endpoints <svc>` / `kubectl get endpointslice`.
- `kubectl expose` copies the Deployment's selector automatically — if you write YAML by hand, you must set the selector yourself.
- `targetPort` defaults to `port`; if your container listens elsewhere, set it explicitly or you'll get connection-refused.
- `sessionAffinity: ClientIP` pins a client to one backend; default is `None` (round-robin-ish).
questions.prompt:
A Deployment `web` (nginx, 3 replicas, label `app=web`) is already running in `cni-learn`. Expose it with a `ClusterIP` Service named `web` on port `80`.

Target: Service `web` exists and has active endpoints.
questions.hint: `kubectl expose deployment web -n cni-learn --name=web --port=80`, then `kubectl get endpoints web -n cni-learn`.
questions.solution:
kubectl expose deployment web -n cni-learn --name=web --port=80
kubectl get endpoints web -n cni-learn   # lists pod IPs

questions.title: Pod-to-pod through the Service
questions.teach:
This is the whole datapath working together, and a great mental checklist for troubleshooting connectivity:
1. **DNS** — the client resolves `web.cni-learn` via CoreDNS to the Service clusterIP.
2. **Service / kube-proxy** — the clusterIP is DNAT'd (iptables/IPVS) to a backend pod IP.
3. **CNI** — the packet crosses the pod network to the backend, and nginx replies.

**How to test each hop in the exam:**
- Name resolves? `nslookup web.cni-learn` (or the FQDN).
- Service reachable? `wget -qO- http://web.cni-learn` or `curl` the clusterIP:port directly.
- Backend alive? `wget` a **pod IP** directly (bypasses the Service) to isolate whether it's a Service/selector problem or a pod problem.

**Short-name vs FQDN:** from a pod in `cni-learn`, `web`, `web.cni-learn`, and `web.cni-learn.svc.cluster.local` all work thanks to the `search` list; from another namespace you need at least `web.cni-learn`.

**Exam gotchas:**
- If `wget` hangs/times out: check Service **endpoints** (empty = selector/readiness issue), then kube-proxy on the node, then a **NetworkPolicy** silently dropping the traffic (default-deny ingress on the backend, or egress on the client — don't forget DNS egress to `kube-system:53`).
- If you get `NXDOMAIN`/`bad address`: it's DNS, not the datapath — the Service name or namespace is wrong.
- busybox `wget` needs `-qO-` to print to stdout; without it you get a downloaded file and empty logs.
- A `Connection refused` (vs timeout) means you reached a pod but hit the wrong `targetPort`.
questions.prompt:
Run a pod named `client` (image `busybox:1.36`) that fetches `http://web.cni-learn` and prints the response.

Target: `client`'s logs show the nginx welcome page (it reached the Service).
questions.hint: `kubectl run client -n cni-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never --command -- wget -qO- http://web.cni-learn`, then `kubectl logs client -n cni-learn`.
questions.solution:
kubectl run client -n cni-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never --command -- wget -qO- http://web.cni-learn
kubectl logs client -n cni-learn   # <title>Welcome to nginx!</title>

verification.description: client reached the web Service (full CNI + kube-proxy datapath)
